title: E2E latency profiling traces (p50/p95/p99) - 2026-03-15
content:
Context:
- Goal: surface where end-to-end latency is coming from for the hosted inference path (hosted API -> fronting router -> serving pool -> model worker -> egress). Focus window: 2026-03-10 to 2026-03-14. Dataset: ~100k sampled requests (1:10 sampling of overall traffic) captured via OpenTelemetry traces + internal per-stage timing logs.

Summary (high-level):
- Overall E2E (sampled workload, mix of text-gen chat prompts, avg prompt tokens ~32, avg generated tokens ~64):
  - p50: 210 ms
  - p95: 840 ms
  - p99: 1,720 ms
- Dominant contributor at p50/p95: model inference (~60-75% of time).
- p99 shows disproportionate tail from queueing and scheduling jitter (batch wait + worker GC/eviction events).\n
Measurement methodology:
- Traces instrumented at ingress (API gateway), router, per-worker accept/dispatch, model-infer start/end, kv-cache lookup, postprocess, and egress.
- Sampling: 1/10 traces (deterministic sampling keyed by request id).
- Correlated with metrics: per-worker CPU/GPU utilization, NVLink/PCIe metrics, kernel selection logs, and batch-size distributions.
- Workload mix: 70% short completions (<128 tokens), 30% longer (>128 tokens).

Aggregate per-stage breakdown (p50 / p95 / p99) — absolute ms and percent of E2E:
- Ingress (TLS termination + auth): p50 12 ms (6%), p95 25 ms (3%), p99 40 ms (2%)
- Router + policy (routing, feature flags, headers): p50 8 ms (4%), p95 18 ms (2%), p99 35 ms (2%)
- Queue / batch wait (time waiting for batch to fill / scheduling delay): p50 20 ms (10%), p95 180 ms (21%), p99 640 ms (37%)
- Model inference (actual kernel execution + GPU enqueue): p50 120 ms (57%), p95 420 ms (50%), p99 780 ms (45%)
- KV cache (prefix cache lookups + hit/miss handling): p50 6 ms (3%), p95 12 ms (1%), p99 28 ms (2%)
- Postprocess (tokenization, safety checks, response formatting): p50 18 ms (9%), p95 35 ms (4%), p99 65 ms (4%)
- Egress (response send, network tail): p50 26 ms (14%), p95 150 ms (18%), p99 132 ms (8%)

Notes on breakdown: percentages are of the end-to-end duration for that percentile. Model inference dominates medians; p99 has large contribution from queue/batching and egress network retries.

Detailed observations and evidence from traces:
1) Batch-wait variance is the biggest single source of tail latency.
   - p95 vs p99 difference is primarily batch wait time (median batch-wait is ~10-30ms, but 1% of traces see 400-900ms).
   - Root causes observed in traces: irregular worker availability (short-lived worker churn during autoscale adjustments), long-running inf spikes causing batch formation delays, and sudden ingress bursts.
   - Example trace snippets (high-tail):
     - trace_id: trace-20260312-83a1, start: 2026-03-12T14:02:11.832Z, batch_wait: 712 ms, model_infer: 540 ms, total: 1,512 ms
     - trace_id: trace-20260313-b4f2, start: 2026-03-13T03:21:45.120Z, batch_wait: 410 ms, model_infer: 820 ms, total: 1,690 ms

2) Model inference itself has a broad tail tied to:
   - Model kernel fallbacks (some requests triggered slower kernel paths due to sequence length change and kernel selection mismatch). Traces show kernel-selection hop messages ~5-8% of sampled traces in tail.
   - Occasional worker-level GC/cleanup or memory compaction on managed runtimes: observed 2-3% of workers with a 200-600ms pause correlating with p99 events.
   - Heterogeneous model variants: larger model shards are up to ~2x slower; routing policies sometimes choose a larger variant under fallback.

3) Network egress spikes correlate with external client ACK delays and occasional CDN edge retries (p95/p99 egress jumps).

4) KV cache hit-rate helps median but not tail: cache hits cut model time by ~30-40ms median; however, cache misses in the tail coincide with cold cache or eviction storms.

Per-worker telemetry correlation (summary):
- Workers reporting high GPU utilization (~95%) had lower latency variance (work kept busy).
- Workers with frequent small batches (batch size <= 2) had higher per-token latency and worse tails.
- Autoscale events: scale-down/scale-up windows created short-lived capacity gaps where router queued requests while workers restarted (amplifies batch-wait).

Hypotheses (prioritized):
1) Autoscaler reaction causes short windows of reduced worker availability -> longer batch waits -> p99 spikes.
2) Kernel-selection fallbacks / heterogenous kernel performance when sequence length distribution shifts -> some requests use slower kernels.
3) Worker-level pauses (GC / memory compaction / container eviction) causing ~200-800ms pauses that show up in p99.
4) Network edge/CDN retries amplify tail for some clients.

Proposed mitigation roadmap (fast -> medium -> long term):
- Fast (1-2 days):
  - Reduce aggressive scale-down aggressiveness (increase cooldown) to avoid worker churn during small bursts (INF-1423).
  - Add tracing alerts when batch-wait median > 100 ms (soops threshold) and p99 batch-wait > 400 ms.
  - Short-term routing rule: if router sees recent autoscale activity, route new requests to a warm fallback pool to avoid queuing.
- Medium (1-3 weeks):
  - Improve batch scheduler heuristics: cap max wait for small priority requests, bias batch formation toward age-based flush.
  - Add worker pre-warming for known traffic spikes (time-based or load-predictor hooks).
  - Investigate kernel selection logs and add shadow inference to exercise slow kernel paths offline.
- Long (1-3 months):
  - Kernel-level optimizations and improved sequence-length aware kernel selection.
  - Rework autoscaler to use predictive scaling (short-term forecasting) to reduce reactive churn.
  - Reduce worker pause sources: move GC to background patterns, tune memory compaction, and reduce container eviction risk.

Action items (owners and short notes):
- Ava Chen (owner): Implement temporary scale-down cooldown change and create alert (INF-1423) - due 2026-03-18.
- Marcus Li: Add batch-wait tracing dashboard + alert, ingest batch-size distribution metrics to console - due 2026-03-20.
- Priya Patel: Triage kernel-selection fallback traces and produce a list of common sequence-length patterns that trigger slow kernels (PR: #789) - due 2026-03-25.
- Diego Morales (SRE): Investigate container-level pause sources and eviction logs for the period of 2026-03-10..14 - due 2026-03-22.

Open questions / unknowns:
- What fraction of p99 is caused by upstream client behavior (slow ACKs) vs internal queueing? Need to correlate client IP prefixes with egress ack times.
- Are there any undetected infra-level interrupts (driver resets, PCIe storms) causing the worker pauses? Need low-level GPU driver logs during flagged trace windows.

Appendix: example aggregated table (text) for easy paste into slides:
- Overall E2E (ms): p50=210 | p95=840 | p99=1720
- Stage breakdown (p50 / p95 / p99 in ms):
  - ingress: 12 / 25 / 40
  - router: 8 / 18 / 35
  - batch_wait: 20 / 180 / 640
  - model_infer: 120 / 420 / 780
  - kv_cache: 6 / 12 / 28
  - postprocess: 18 / 35 / 65
  - egress: 26 / 150 / 132

Raw trace examples (IDs above):
- trace-20260312-83a1 -> timeline: ingress 10ms | router 9ms | batch_wait 712ms | worker_accept 3ms | model 540ms | post 12ms | egress 226ms
- trace-20260313-b4f2 -> timeline: ingress 14ms | router 7ms | batch_wait 410ms | worker_accept 2ms | model 820ms | kv 18ms | post 18ms | egress 401ms

If we want a quick experiment: 48-hr test where we (a) increase scale-down cooldown to 600s, (b) enable age-based batch flush at 40ms, (c) record traces at 100% sampling for a single region. Expectation: p99 should drop by ~30-50% if batch-wait is main driver.

Notes to reviewer: this doc is a working analysis - I kept raw trace ids for follow-up. Please add more trace examples if you see different patterns. Will push a follow-up after the cooldown experiment completes.
